newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW - Daiichi Pharm aims to maintain growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Daiichi Pharm aims to maintain growth.

text.p: Daiichi Pharmaceutical Co Ltd expects to post a record profit for the business year which ended on March 31, and says it will aim to keep annual earnings growing at a pace of four to five percent.
"Our parent current profit for 1996/97 is forecast to hit a record high, breaking the previous record seven years ago," company president Tadashi Suzuki told Reuters in a recent interview.
Daiichi, one of Japan's leading drug companies, expects to post a parent current profit of about 44.13 billion yen ($370 million) in the year to March 31, 1997, up 3.2 percent from the previous year.
Sales are forecast to rise five percent in 1996/97 from a year earlier, Suzuki said.
For this 1997/98 business year, parent current profits are expected to grow by 4.2 percent year-on-year, Suzuki said.
Current profit is pre-tax profit including gains and losses on non-operating activities such as securities investments.
With profits growing firmly, Daiichi plans to increase annual dividends by two yen to 18 yen this year, he said.
Japan's medical industry is currently facing an increasingly harsh business environment with the government cutting medical expenditure.

However, Suzuki said Daiichi would endeavour to keep profits growing at an annual four to five percent and that the company was moving ahead with various measures, such as expanding overseas operations and developing new products to weather the changing environment.
"Our strategy for the medium-term will be to try maintain current prices for our products, expand business overseas and develop profitable products," Suzuki said.
Suzuki said overseas operations were an especially important element of Daiichi's business.
Sales at the firm's overseas division rose by an annual 14 percent last business year, and double-digit growth is expected to continue over the medium-term, Suzuki said.
Daiichi is aiming for overseas sales to account for 20 percent of its total sales and 30 percent of its profit, up from 1996/97's 10.4 percent and 16 percent.
"Overseas operations are strategically important for us and we may carry out merger and acquisition activities if necessary," Suzuki said.

"Over the long term, China is an attractive market," Suzuki said, adding that he wanted to boost exports to the country to 10 billion yen ($84.0 million) by 2000/01 from about 2.7 billion yen ($22.6 million) last year.
Daiichi may set up a production plant in China once it confirms sales there will grow, Suzuki said.
Daiichi's investment in research and development is only about 13 percent of its annual sales, Suzuki said.

Although the amount was small compared to giant drug makers overseas, Daiichi would compete by focusing development on medicine for digestive and circulatory organs, infection, anti-cancer drugs and X-ray contrast media, he said.

On areas of prospective growth, Suzuki said exports of the synthetic antibacterial drug "Cravit" to Britain were likely to start in the third quarter of this year, following its launch in the United States earlier this year.
Daiichi would probably be able to export "Cravit" to several other European countries in early 1998, he said.

He said the outlook for Daichi's cerebral function activator "Translon", due to be launched in Japan this year, was promising, and that the company would probably be able to sell Translon overseas within a few years.
